title: The Free Salters' Pay-Board
author: the Salt-King's clerk
body:
# Pay, this week

*In sacks. A sack is four stone. Four stone is what the old reeve's board cannot see.*

| hand | boat | sacks |
|---|---|---|
| H. Kettle | the Two Pins | 3 |
| D. Aske | the Gull | 2 |
| W. Mew | the Merry Tally | 4 |
| S. Aske | (on foot) | 1 |
| the Hush-wife's man | (by night) | 6 |

*W. Mew's boat to be broken up for the cut's shoring, her name-board kept for the brass. He is not to go home. He knows it.*

*Below, in another hand, pressed hard:* Tell my mother nothing. -- W.

title: To the Gulls of the Saltmound
author: Hesketh Vane, by his own appointment King of Salt
body:
# To the Gulls

Madams,

You have the top of the mound and I have its heart. You have the Charter's salt and so have I, and neither of us has paid for it. I have taken six years and four stone at a time, and the old reeve has never seen me, because a Tallyman looks at a seal and not at a mountain.

The Charter says the salt is the city's because it came ashore here. The sea says it was the sea's. The Salt Isles say it was theirs. I say it is whoever's carries it, and I carry it, and so it is mine, and I am King of it.

You may keep the top.

*Your servant in all things but the salt,*
H. V.

title: The Patience, Dive-Log
author: Corwen Lisle, Master
body:
# The Patience, the last dives

**12th.** Down to the Bell Street. Dry as ever. Raised two bronze lamps and a piece of a door. The Undersong is hanging where it always hangs, at the bottom of the Singing Stair. Did not go near.

**19th.** Down. The Sayers' factor has offered more for the Undersong than the Company is worth. Went to the head of the Singing Stair and looked. It is still. Its tongue is in it. Came up.

**26th.** Down with Pryor, the two Moyles, Bean. For the Undersong.

*Later, in the same hand, smaller, the ink run as if wet:*

We took the tongue out of it and it rang anyway. Not struck. Rang. The Quarter's water came up the low side of the street to listen. Pryor and Bean went down the stair to it and did not come back up, and they are still down there, walking slowly, holding their breath, and so are the Moyles now.

It has to be struck back. If it is struck it stops. If I strike it, it stops.

Tell Merryn to wind the chain a quarter every hour so it does not set.

title: A Street-Plate of the Drowned Quarter
author: the Builders; read by the Fathom Company
body:
# A Street-Plate

*Black stone, cut deep, the signs as sharp as the day they were cut. On the back, in salvors' chalk, the Company's reading, which they admit is a guess:*

THE STREET OF THE HELD BREATH.
THE WATER WAITS AT THE DOOR.
STRIKE NOTHING THAT IS SINGING.

*Under it, in Corwen Lisle's hand:* We have been reading the third line wrong for sixty years. We read it STRIKE NOTHING, SINGING. -- C.L.
